questions.q: What does the book mean by strategic incompetence?
a: Deliberately accepting weak spots so your strengths get the time
Pretending to be bad at tasks so others will not ask for help
Hiring experts for every part of a project from day one
Refusing to learn any skill outside your main profession
questions.why: Lesson 1 says choosing where to be incompetent lets you prioritize what you do well.

questions.q: What should you do when self-doubt strikes just before launching?
a: Ship the work anyway, because few will notice the final polish
Delay the launch until every small flaw has been fixed
Show it to a large test audience before deciding
Start over with a completely different approach
questions.why: Lesson 2 says the last few percent of perfection rarely matter to readers.

questions.q: Why is that last-minute doubting voice so hard to ignore?
a: It is partly right that more time would improve the work
It comes from people who genuinely want you to fail
It only appears when the project is truly unfinished
It accurately predicts how most audiences will react
questions.why: Lesson 2 admits the voice has a point, yet the gain is usually invisible.

questions.q: When does the summary say you should check your progress numbers?
a: Periodically, such as weekly or monthly, not several times a day
Every morning before starting any creative work
Only after a project has been finished and published
Whenever a friend or competitor posts something new
questions.why: Lesson 3 says tracking helps at the right intervals and can destroy momentum daily.

questions.q: What trick does perfectionism use to make you feel behind?
a: It claims you are not making enough progress without defining enough
It compares your first draft with a finished masterpiece
It hides your statistics so you cannot see any growth
It convinces you that your audience has stopped growing
questions.why: Lesson 3 says we often never decide what enough progress would look like.
